newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH UNVEIL EUTHANASIA REFORM, STOP SHORT OF LAW.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH UNVEIL EUTHANASIA REFORM, STOP SHORT OF LAW.

text.p: The Netherlands on Tuesday unveiled steps to further decriminalise euthanasia, but said the time was not yet ripe for legalised mercy killing on request.

"There are no plans to amend the criminal code (to legalise euthanasia) because...public debate on the issue has not been rounded off. Public feeling about euthanasia must stabilise," Justice Minister Winnie Sorgdrager told a news conference.

Dutch right-to-die campaigners and doctors have pressed the government for changes in the law to guarantee freedom of prosecution for doctors performing euthanasia under strictly controlled conditions.
Current Dutch law offers no such immunity, although euthanasia is tolerated if certain guidelines are followed.
Under the guidelines, patients must have been of sound mind, in unbearable physical or mental pain and have repeatedly asked for death.
Before ending a patient's life, a doctor must consult a second, independent, physician.
In 1995, Dutch doctors reported 1,466 cases of euthanasia, but a further 2,734 cases went unreported because doctors feared prosecution, a government inquiry reported last November.

Under the new measures unveiled on Tuesday, reported euthanasia cases will no longer automatically be referred to the Public Prosecutor but will be submitted to an independent committee of medical, legal and ethical experts.

These regional evaluation committees will assess whether euthanising doctors have taken due care in meeting a patient's death-request and, where necessary, could refer doubtful cases to the Public Prosecutor, Sorgdrager said.
"The nature of criminal law is very black and white...we need a more nuanced assessment (of euthanasia cases)," she said.
"This (new) way of assessing cases will lower the reporting threshold for euthanising doctors while, at the same time, the committees will have an educative function," she said.
Although technically a doctor could still be prosecuted even if the committee found he had acted with due care, in practice this would be extremely unlikely, the minister said.
"The cabinet believes the proposed measures will...enhance the legal security of both patient and doctor," she said.
The new reporting procedures fall far short of the law changes sought by pro-euthanasia campaigners and the Dutch professional medical council (KNMG).

KNMG said in a statement that it supported the cabinet's proposals for regional committees but added it was disappointed at the government's failure to guarantee euthanising doctors freedom from prosecution.

"KNMG is disappointed that...(its) wishes have not been met for an amendment to the criminal code which lays down that doctors acting in accordance with the due-care criteria are absolved from prosecution," it said.
But Sorgdrager said that at an estimated four in 10, the incidence of reported euthanasia was still too low to justify institutionalising mercy-killing practice.
Nor could euthanasia be legalised within a context of insufficient palliative care for terminal patients, Health Minister Els Borst said.
"We must never allow ourselves to run the risk of a doctor and patient deciding on euthanasia because the doctor has insufficient knowledge of the alternatives," she said.
